316.title: Peace with God (Romans 5:1–11)
316.hook: suffering, patience, character, hope; while we were still sinners, Christ died
316.howItsDone: Christians often turn to Romans 5:1–5 in illness or loss; chaplains and friends read it with people in a hard season, and look back together on what that season grew.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was faith, pistis, trust: an old man under the stars, and your line was counted as right. Did you open your hand on the thing you were gripping? Day three hundred sixteen.

Ask the steady one in your life how they got that way, the one people call at two in the morning. The answer is rarely: everything went well for me. More often it's: the year my dad was sick. The job I lost. The long winter after the divorce. Something hard happened, and something grew in the hard ground. Nobody chooses the hard part. But what grew is often what they'd keep. Paul knew this pattern from the inside. He'd been shipwrecked, beaten, jailed, and he was still writing letters. In Romans chapter five he traces the pattern step by step, and he starts it somewhere surprising: with peace.
screen: `HOW DID THEY GET THAT WAY?` → `SOMETHING HARD HAPPENED.` → `PAUL STARTS WITH PEACE.`

segments.voice: Chapter five opens, in the King James Bible: "Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ." The Greek word for peace is eirene, and behind it stands the Hebrew shalom: not just no fighting, but wholeness, everything in its right place. After four chapters about guilt and grace, this is where Paul lands. The war is over. Then he does something odd. He says we glory, we even boast, in tribulations. Not because suffering is good. Because of what can grow in it. Listen to the chain: "tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope: And hope maketh not ashamed." Four links. Hard times grow endurance. Endurance grows what the King James calls experience; the Greek means tested character, like metal that's been through the fire and proved true. And that tested character grows hope. And hope, Paul says, doesn't let you down. Maketh not ashamed: an echo of Paul's opening a few days ago, not ashamed. Why doesn't it disappoint? Because, he says, the love of God has been poured into our hearts. Then comes the line that holds the whole chapter up: "But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." Not after we got better. While. Paul notes that hardly anyone would die even for a righteous person. This love didn't wait for anyone to deserve it. Some readers say the chain is easier to see looking back than from the middle of it.
screen: `EIRENE: SHALOM, WHOLENESS.` · `GLORY IN TRIBULATIONS.` · `PATIENCE, TESTED CHARACTER, HOPE.` · `WHILE WE WERE YET SINNERS.` · then, large: `HOPE MAKETH NOT ASHAMED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: list one hardship that grew you. Settle, and breathe. Go back through your life slowly and find one hard season that, looking back, grew something in you. Patience. Compassion. Honesty. A friend you'd never have met. Don't pretend it was good; it may still hurt. Just name the hardship, and then name what grew. If a hardship you're in right now comes to mind instead, let it be there too, without forcing any lesson on it yet. If you pray, you can give thanks for what grew, and ask for hope in what hasn't yet. The bell holds the time.
Eirene. Paul's Greek word for peace, carrying the Hebrew shalom: wholeness, the war over, everything in its right place.
Your line: hope does not disappoint. Today, tell one person about a hard season that grew something in you, or ask them about theirs. Day three hundred sixteen.

317.title: Adam and Christ (Romans 5:12–21)
317.hook: where sin increased, grace abounded all the more
317.howItsDone: Christians read Romans 5 when they teach about sin and salvation, and in the Easter Vigil's ancient hymn, the Exsultet, Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran churches sing of Adam's fall and of the grace that came after it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, peace with God, eirene, and the chain from tribulation to hope. Your line was hope does not disappoint. Did you tell someone about a hard season that grew you? Day three hundred seventeen.

Some things you inherit without asking. Your grandmother's nose. Your family's way of going quiet when things get tense. A house, or a debt. You didn't choose any of it, and it shapes you anyway. Paul, in the second half of Romans chapter five, steps way back from Rome and from his own day, all the way back to the garden in Genesis. He's thinking about the whole human family and what it has inherited. And he sets two figures side by side, like two ends of a seesaw: the first man, and one more. Today is those two names.
screen: `THINGS YOU INHERIT WITHOUT ASKING.` → `BACK TO THE GARDEN.` → `TWO FIGURES, SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: Paul begins, in the King James Bible: "Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned." One man, Adam, opened a door, and sin and death came through it into the whole human story. Then Paul sets up the other end of the seesaw: "For as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous." Adam and Christ. One disobeyed, one obeyed. One brought death, one brings life. But here's what Paul keeps insisting: it isn't an even seesaw. Again and again he says much more. The gift is not like the fall. Then comes the line of the day: "But where sin abounded, grace did much more abound." Paul is so eager here he reaches for a super-word in Greek: grace super-abounded, over-overflowed. However big the mess gets, grace is bigger. Now, Christians understand the Adam side differently, so here's who says what. In the West, following Augustine, Catholics and the churches of the Reformation speak of original sin: every person is born sharing in Adam's fallen state, even in some sense his guilt. Orthodox Christians usually speak of ancestral sin: we inherit mortality and a wounded nature, but not Adam's personal guilt. Some scholars trace part of that difference to how one small phrase in this passage was translated into Latin. Either way, Paul's direction of travel is plain. The chapter doesn't end with Adam. It ends with grace reigning, through Jesus Christ.
screen: `BY ONE MAN SIN ENTERED.` · `BY THE OBEDIENCE OF ONE.` · `NOT AN EVEN SEESAW: MUCH MORE.` · `ORIGINAL SIN, ANCESTRAL SIN.` · then, large: `GRACE DID MUCH MORE ABOUND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice grace bigger than a mistake. Settle, and breathe. Think of a mistake, yours or someone else's, that turned out to be smaller than what came after it. A fight that ended in a better friendship. A wrong turn that led somewhere good. Someone who forgave you more than you expected. Don't explain it away. Just let yourself see that the mistake wasn't the end of the story. Breathe out, and let that sink in. If you pray, you can thank God for that grace, by name. The bell holds the time.
Charis. Paul's Greek word for grace: a gift freely given, which he says super-abounds wherever sin abounds.
Your line: grace abounds. Today, when a mistake, yours or someone else's, looks like the end of the story, say those two words under your breath. Day three hundred seventeen.

what it means: Paul sets them side by side: one opened the door to sin and death, one to life, and grace is always the heavier side.
what a scholar hears: Paul's Greek eph' hō in 5:12 likely means because all sinned, but the Latin Bible read in whom all sinned, which shaped Augustine's teaching on original sin.

318.title: Dead to sin (Romans 6)
318.hook: baptism as burial and rising: walk in newness of life
318.howItsDone: Romans 6:3–11 is often read at baptisms and at the Easter Vigil, and some Christians touch water on entering church, or recall their baptism each morning, as a reminder of dying and rising with Christ.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Adam and Christ on Paul's seesaw, and charis, and your line was grace abounds. Did a mistake look like the end of the story, and did you answer it? Day three hundred eighteen.

A kid has just been told: whatever you break, it's already forgiven. For a moment the kid looks thoughtful. Then the kid looks at the china cabinet. Paul saw this coming. He's just said that where sin abounded, grace did much more abound, and he can hear someone in the back of the room raising a hand. Wait. If more sin means more grace, shouldn't we sin more? Give grace something to do? It's a sharp question, and maybe some people in Rome were really asking it. Paul answers with two words, and then with a picture of water, a grave and a morning. That picture is today.
screen: `WHATEVER YOU BREAK IS FORGIVEN.` → `SO SHOULD WE SIN MORE?` → `WATER, A GRAVE, A MORNING.`

segments.voice: Here's the question, in the King James Bible: "What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid." In Greek, me genoito: absolutely not, may it never be. Then Paul reaches for baptism. The Greek word baptizo means to dip, to plunge under. And Paul says going under the water is like going into a grave. "Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life." So the old life, the one run by sin, has been buried. You don't go back to the grave to live there. You walk out into a new morning. That's what dead to sin means for Paul: not that temptation disappears, but that it no longer owns you. He talks about slavery, a picture Paul's hearers in Rome saw every day: you used to belong to one master, now you belong to another. And he ends the chapter with a line that sums up the chapter: "For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord." Wages are earned. A gift is not. Churches practice baptism in different ways, so here's who says what. Catholics, Orthodox Christians, and Protestant churches such as Lutherans, Anglicans, Methodists and Presbyterians baptize babies as well as adults, trusting God's grace comes first. Baptists, Pentecostals and others baptize only those old enough to confess faith themselves. Some pour water, some plunge the whole body under, and the Orthodox immerse even infants three times. And Romans 6 is often read at baptisms, because the picture is the same: down into the water, up into new life.
screen: `SHALL WE CONTINUE IN SIN? GOD FORBID.` · `BAPTIZO: PLUNGED UNDER.` · `BURIED WITH HIM, RAISED TO WALK.` · `WAGES EARNED, A GIFT GIVEN.` · then, large: `WALK IN NEWNESS OF LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: start one new habit. Settle, and breathe. Think of one small thing that belongs to an old way of living you'd like to leave behind. Scrolling the minute you wake up. A sharp tone with someone at home. Picture it going under, like the water in Paul's picture. Then picture what you'd do instead, one small, new thing, and see yourself doing it tomorrow morning. Make it tiny enough to actually start. If you pray, you can ask for help to walk in it. The bell holds the time.
Baptizo. The Greek word for baptism: to dip, to plunge under, like going down into a grave and walking out new.
Your line: newness of life. Today, the next time you wash your hands or your face, let the water remind you of the one new habit you've chosen, and do it once. Day three hundred eighteen.

what a scholar hears: early Christian baptism was often full immersion, which makes Paul's burial picture vivid, and the Greek wages, opsōnia, was a soldier's pay.

319.title: The wretched man (Romans 7:14–25)
319.hook: the good I want, I don't do
319.howItsDone: Christians often turn to Romans 7 when talking honestly about habits and temptation, in confession, in recovery groups and in spiritual direction, where the struggle is named without shame.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dead to sin, baptizo, a burial and a rising, and your line was newness of life. Did you try your one new habit? If it wobbled already, today is for you. Day three hundred nineteen.

The alarm is set for six. The running shoes are by the door. The plan was made with a clear head and good intentions. Then six o'clock comes, and a hand reaches over and turns the alarm off. Or it's the sharp word someone swore they wouldn't say, and there it is, out loud again. Wanting one thing and doing another is an old and ordinary human knot. What's surprising is to find it in the middle of Paul's letter to Rome, right after his big picture of new life. He stops arguing, and writes in the first person about a war inside him.
screen: `THE ALARM, THE SHOES, THE SNOOZE.` → `WANTING ONE THING, DOING ANOTHER.` → `PAUL WRITES IN THE FIRST PERSON.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in the King James Bible: "For the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do." Read it twice; it doubles back on itself like the knot it describes. Paul says he agrees with God's law. He delights in it. He knows it's good. And still, something in him pulls the other way, like a second law at war inside him. The knowing isn't the problem. The doing is. Then the paragraph breaks open into a cry: "O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?" Wretched, in Greek talaiporos, means miserable, worn down by hardship. It isn't a pose. It's a groan. And notice the question he asks. Not how do I fix myself, but who shall deliver me? He's looking outside himself. And the answer comes in the very next breath: "I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord." Now here's a real puzzle, one Christians have argued over for a long time: who is this I? Some readers, including Augustine in his later years and Martin Luther, hear Paul describing the Christian life: even the baptized still feel this war inside, every day. Other readers, among them early Greek teachers and scholars today, hear Paul speaking about life under the law without the Spirit, the way things look before chapter eight. The text doesn't settle it for us. Either way, Paul writes it in the present tense, and he doesn't flinch. His letter doesn't hide the struggle or scold it. It names it, and it cries out for help.
screen: `THE GOOD THAT I WOULD I DO NOT.` · `TWO LAWS AT WAR INSIDE.` · `WHO SHALL DELIVER ME?` · `WHO IS THIS I?` · then, large: `O WRETCHED MAN THAT I AM!`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be gentle with your own struggle. Settle, and breathe. Name one thing you keep doing that you don't want to do. Something small and real. Instead of the usual lecture you give yourself, try speaking to yourself the way you'd speak to a friend who told you the same thing. Tired. Honest. Still trying. Notice where the struggle sits in your body, and let your breath go there. If you pray, you can say Paul's own question, who shall deliver me, and just wait with it. The bell holds the time.
Talaiporos. Paul's Greek cry of wretchedness: worn down by the war between the good he wants and what he does.

Your line: who shall deliver me? Today, when you catch yourself doing the thing you didn't want to do, skip the lecture. Take one breath, and ask for help, from God or from a friend. Day three hundred nineteen.

320.title: No condemnation (Romans 8:1–17)
320.hook: there is now no condemnation; we cry Abba, Father
320.carry: a child at home, not a prisoner on trial
320.howItsDone: Many Christians memorize Romans 8:1, and many use the word Abba in personal prayer, the way Jesus did in the garden; Romans 8 is often read at baptisms and funerals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the wretched man, talaiporos: the good I want, I don't do. Your line was who shall deliver me? Did you ask for help instead of giving yourself a lecture? Day three hundred twenty.

Some people carry a courtroom around inside their heads. A prosecutor who never takes a day off. You forgot the birthday: guilty. You snapped at the kids: guilty. That thing from ninth grade: still guilty, somehow, at three in the morning. The case is never closed. Yesterday Paul ended chapter seven crying out, who shall deliver me? Today he turns the page, and chapter eight, which many readers call the high point of the whole letter, opens with a verdict. It's short. It's the first thing he says. And for the prosecutor in your head, it's very bad news.
screen: `A COURTROOM INSIDE YOUR HEAD.` → `THE CASE IS NEVER CLOSED.` → `CHAPTER EIGHT OPENS WITH A VERDICT.`

segments.voice: Here's the verdict, in the King James Bible: "There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus." No condemnation. The Greek word is katakrima, and it's more than a guilty verdict; it's the sentence that follows, the penalty handed down. Paul says there is none. Not less. None. And not someday: now. The word now echoes the hinge from a few days ago, but now. Then Paul explains how: the Spirit. In chapter seven the Spirit was hardly mentioned; in chapter eight the Spirit is everywhere, living in people, giving life, leading them. And then the courtroom turns into a family room: "For ye have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear; but ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father." Abba is Aramaic, the language Jesus spoke at home. It's the word a child uses for a father, close and warm, and Mark's Gospel says Jesus himself prayed Abba in the garden the night before he died. Paul keeps it in Aramaic even when writing in Greek to Rome, as if some words shouldn't be translated. And adoption was a serious thing in Roman law: an adopted son became a full heir, with a new name and a new standing. Paul goes on: the Spirit itself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God. So the prosecutor doesn't get the last word. A father does. Christians of every church say that doesn't make wrong things right; it means a person isn't defined by them. You can still say sorry. You can still change. But you do it as a child at home, not as a prisoner on trial.
screen: `KATAKRIMA: THE SENTENCE HANDED DOWN.` · `NOW: NOT SOMEDAY.` · `THE SPIRIT OF ADOPTION.` · `ABBA: A CHILD'S WORD FOR FATHER.` · then, large: `THERE IS THEREFORE NOW NO CONDEMNATION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: drop one old self-accusation. Settle, and breathe. Listen for the prosecutor in your head, and find one charge it keeps bringing up. Something old, something you've already apologized for, or can't fix now. Hear it clearly, once. Then imagine the case being closed. The file set down. On each breath out, let the charge go a little further away. If it comes back, that's all right; set it down again. If you pray, you can say the old family word, Abba, and rest there. The bell holds the time.
No condemnation. Katakrima in Greek: the sentence, the penalty. Paul says for those in Christ there is none, and there is none now.
Your line: a child at home, not a prisoner on trial. Today, when the old charge comes back, answer it by living like a child at home, and then do one kind thing. Day three hundred twenty.

321.title: Groaning creation (Romans 8:18–27)
321.hook: the whole creation groans in labor; the Spirit prays in groans too deep for words
321.howItsDone: Some Christians lean on Romans 8:26 when they cannot find words, praying in silence, with tears or with a sigh; some Pentecostal and charismatic Christians also connect it with praying in tongues.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a verdict and a family word: Abba, Father. Your line was a child at home, not a prisoner on trial. When the old charge came back, did you answer it? Day three hundred twenty-one.
screen: `A CHILD AT HOME, NOT A PRISONER ON TRIAL.`

segments.voice: A hospital room, late. Someone sits beside the bed with nothing left to say. Outside, after the bad news, all that comes out is a long breath, not quite a word. Prayer is often pictured as sentences: nicely put, in the right order. Then comes a moment when the sentences are gone. Paul, in the middle of Romans chapter eight, stops to talk about exactly that. And he widens it. It isn't only one person who groans, he says. It's the whole world. And then he says something about God and the prayers that have no words.
screen: `A HOSPITAL ROOM, NOTHING TO SAY.` → `A BREATH THAT ISN'T QUITE A WORD.` → `THE WHOLE WORLD GROANS.`

segments.voice: Paul starts honestly: there is suffering now. "For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us." He doesn't deny the suffering. He sets it beside something bigger. Then he turns to the whole created world, the oceans and forests and animals, and says it's waiting too. The King James calls it the earnest expectation of the creature: like someone on tiptoe at a window. And then: "For we know that the whole creation groaneth and travaileth in pain together until now." Travaileth means the pains of labor. So the groaning isn't a death rattle; it's a birth. Something new is coming, and the world is in labor with it. Then Paul brings it home, to us, to the hospital room: "Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities: for we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered." Three groans, then. Creation groans. We groan. And, Paul says, the Spirit of God groans with us, underneath our words, when we have none. Paul admits something here that's easy to miss: we don't know how to pray as we ought. Even Paul. For him, the prayer doesn't depend on getting the words right. Some Christians say this verse gives them permission to pray with tears, or a sigh, or silence. Some Pentecostal and charismatic Christians connect it with praying in tongues; others read it as the silent prayer of the heart. Both readings find the same promise in it: nobody groans alone.
screen: `SUFFERING NOW, GLORY COMING.` · `CREATION ON TIPTOE.` · `LABOR PAINS, NOT DEATH PAINS.` · `THE SPIRIT GROANS WITH US.` · then, large: `GROANINGS WHICH CANNOT BE UTTERED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sigh a prayer without words. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something too big or too tangled to put into sentences. A person who's sick. The state of the world. Something in you that you can't name. Don't try to explain it. Just breathe in, and let out one long, slow sigh. Then another. If you pray, let the sigh be the prayer, and remember what Paul says: that the Spirit is praying with it. If you don't, simply let the sighs carry what words can't. The bell holds the time.
Groaning creation. The whole world in labor pains, waiting for something new, and the Spirit groaning with us, too deep for words.
Your line: the spirit prays with us. Today, when you don't know what to say, to God or to someone who's hurting, let a quiet breath or a hand on a shoulder be enough. Day three hundred twenty-one.

322.title: All things work together (Romans 8:28–30)
322.hook: for good, to those who love God
322.carry: a good thread in the weave
322.howItsDone: Some Christians hold onto Romans 8:28 in hard seasons, and pastors often explain it carefully so it isn't used to call suffering good.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the groaning creation, and the Spirit praying in sighs too deep for words. Your line was the spirit prays with us. Did a breath or a hand on a shoulder do what words couldn't? Day three hundred twenty-two.

It shows up on mugs and sympathy cards, and at funerals, said by someone trying to help: everything happens for a reason. Sometimes it lands gently. Sometimes it lands like a slap. Tell someone whose child is sick that it's all for a reason, and watch their face. Some people assume the line comes from the Bible. The verse it gets pinned to is in Romans chapter eight, and that verse says something different. So today, slowly: what does it actually say, and what doesn't it?
screen: `EVERYTHING HAPPENS FOR A REASON?` → `SOMETIMES A SLAP.` → `WHAT DOES THE VERSE ACTUALLY SAY?`

segments.voice: Here it is, in the King James Bible: "And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose." First, what it doesn't say. It doesn't say all things are good. Paul has just spent a whole paragraph on suffering, groaning, a world in labor pains. He's not pretending cancer is good, or cruelty, or loss. Second, what it does say. Work together is one word in Greek, synergei. You can hear our word synergy in it. Things that are not good in themselves are worked together, woven, into something good. A weaver uses dark threads as well as bright ones, and the pattern only shows from the other side. That picture isn't Paul's, but it helps with his word. And look at who does the working. The verse is about those who love God and are called according to his purpose, so some readers hear God as the subject: God works all things together for good. God is the weaver, not luck. Then verses twenty-nine and thirty trace a golden chain: those God foreknew, he predestined, called, justified and glorified. Christians read that chain differently. Reformed Christians, following Calvin, stress God's sovereign choice. Methodists and others, following Wesley, stress that God's foreknowledge leaves room for human freedom. Catholic and Orthodox teaching holds God's grace and human cooperation together. Each of them finds the same comfort in it: the story is held. This has been quite a week: peace with God, Adam and Christ, dead to sin, the wretched man, no condemnation, the groaning world. Today they all get woven together.
screen: `NOT: ALL THINGS ARE GOOD.` · `SYNERGEI: WOVEN TOGETHER.` · `GOD WORKS ALL THINGS TOGETHER.` · `A GOLDEN CHAIN, READ THREE WAYS.` · then, large: `ALL THINGS WORK TOGETHER FOR GOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for good inside a hard thing. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something hard, maybe from this past week. Don't call it good. It may not be. Just look at it gently, the way you'd turn over a woven cloth to see the back. Is there one thread of good worked into it? A kindness someone showed you. Something you learned. A friend who showed up. If you can't find one yet, that's all right; Paul says we know, not that we always see. If you pray, you can hand the hard thing to God, the weaver. The bell holds the time.
Synergei. Paul's Greek word for worked together: not that hard things are good, but that even they get woven into good.
Your line: a good thread in the weave. Today, if someone is hurting, skip everything happens for a reason. Just be one of the good threads in their hard thing. Day three hundred twenty-two.

fork.setup: a friend's child is in the hospital. you want to comfort them with Romans 8:28. what does the verse actually give you?
options: this is good, it happened for a reason.
even this can be woven into good.

fork.reveal: the verse says all things work together for good, not that all things are good. Paul has just spoken of a world groaning in pain.

original.note: Greek: works together, cooperates. the root of our word synergy.

trapdoor: what you thought: everything happens for a reason.
what it means: not that hard things are good, but that God works even hard things together for good for those who love him.
what a scholar hears: several early manuscripts, including one of the oldest papyri, add ho theos, God, as the subject, while other manuscripts leave all things as the subject.
